notes.meaning: Jacob set out on his journey and stopped at Beersheba on the border of Canaan. This place was special because both Abraham and Isaac had worshipped the Lord there. Before leaving the promised land, Jacob offered sacrifices to thank God and to ask for his guidance and blessing.

During the night, God spoke to Jacob in a vision and called his name twice. Jacob immediately answered that he was ready to listen and obey. God came to reassure him at this great turning point in his life, just as he had done many years earlier when Jacob first left home.

God told Jacob not to be afraid of moving his family down to Egypt. Jacob was very old and likely worried about the long trip, the pull of Egyptian false gods, and ancient warnings about his family suffering in a foreign land. God promised that he would build Jacob's family into a great nation while they lived there.

God promised to go with Jacob into Egypt and to bring his family back to the promised land in the future. He also gave Jacob personal comfort by promising that his beloved son Joseph would be at his side when he died and gently close his eyes. Jacob could move forward with peace knowing the Lord was with him.

Jacob got up from Beersheba with fresh courage and strength from God's promise. Because the aged father was weak and elderly, his sons carried him, along with their wives and children, in the wagons Pharaoh had provided. The family worked together to help their father make the long trek.

The family gathered all their farm animals and the goods they had gained while living in Canaan. They did not come as empty-handed beggars, but brought their own belongings with them into Egypt. Jacob led his entire household into this new land just as God directed.

Jacob brought all his children and grandchildren with him so that the whole family stayed together. As the leader of the family, he made sure no one was left behind in Canaan to suffer in the famine. This complete move showed his trust in God's plan for the future.

A record is now given of the names of Jacob's family members who went down to Egypt. It begins with Reuben, who was Jacob's firstborn son. Listing the family members by name reminds us that God knows and values each person in his covenant family.

These verses name the sons of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. One of Simeon's sons, Shaul, is noted as having a Canaanite mother, which was unusual because the family avoided marrying into the local Canaanite tribes. Levi's sons would later become the leaders of the priestly tribe that served the Lord.

Judah's family line is listed, noting that his two oldest sons, Er and Onan, had died earlier in Canaan. Judah's son Perez had two sons named Hezron and Hamul, who were either born on the way or in Egypt shortly after the arrival. Judah's line is especially important because it leads down through history to the birth of Jesus.

These verses list the four sons of Issachar and the three sons of Zebulun. Issachar's first son Tola, whose name means a small worm, was likely a weak baby, yet he grew to head a very large family. God often takes small and weak beginnings and turns them into a mighty work.

This sums up the descendants born through Leah, including Jacob's daughter Dinah. Counting Jacob himself along with the thirty-two children and grandchildren makes a total of thirty-three. God was steadily fulfilling his ancient promise to give Jacob a large family.

These verses record the sons of Gad and the children of Asher, along with Asher's daughter Serah and two grandsons. Serah is specially mentioned, likely because she remained single or held an honored place in the tribe. These men and their children became the founders of large family clans in Israel.

This verse gives the total count of sixteen descendants who came through Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. Every branch of the household was included in the community of God's chosen people. God used all of them together to build up the nation.

Rachel is remembered as Jacob's beloved wife, and her two sons were Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph had two sons born in Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim, through his Egyptian wife Asenath. These two boys were later blessed by Jacob and treated as full leaders of their own tribes.

Benjamin's ten sons and grandsons are listed, bringing the total number of Rachel's direct descendants to fourteen. Benjamin was the youngest brother, but God blessed him with many children to establish his tribe. Each name represents a growing branch of Jacob's household.

Dan had one son named Hushim, and Naphtali had four sons. These were the children and grandchildren born through Rachel's maidservant Bilhah, numbering seven in all. Even with different family backgrounds, all these sons were united into one covenant people.

The family members who traveled directly with Jacob numbered sixty-six, not counting the wives of his sons. When Jacob, Joseph, and Joseph's two sons are counted, the whole household of Jacob came to seventy people. Over two centuries had passed since God promised Abraham a great nation, and this small group of seventy was the starting point for that great multitude.

Jacob sent Judah ahead of the group to meet Joseph and get instructions about where they should settle in Goshen. Judah had proven himself to be a trustworthy and caring leader among his brothers. Going through proper channels showed respect to the Egyptian authorities who were welcoming them.

Joseph got into his chariot and traveled to Goshen to greet his father. When they met, Joseph threw his arms around his father's neck and wept for joy for a long time. Even though Joseph was a powerful ruler, he showed deep love and honor to his aging father.

Jacob told Joseph that he was now ready to die in peace, because he had seen Joseph's face and knew he was alive. His deepest sorrow was finally turned into complete joy. He felt his life's longings were answered, though God would grant him seventeen more years with his family.

Joseph told his family that he would go speak to Pharaoh to report their arrival. He planned to tell Pharaoh honestly that they were shepherds and had brought all their herds and belongings with them. Joseph acted as their advocate, openly presenting who they were without any shame.

Joseph told his brothers to tell Pharaoh plainly that they had raised livestock all their lives. Egyptians looked down on shepherds, but this difference would work for their good by securing them the rich pastureland of Goshen. Living apart from the Egyptians protected God's people from false worship and kept them united as one nation.
